## TL;DR

Reproduced and fixed the Hub’s dark-mode sidebar mismatch and narrow server list. The shell now resolves semantic AppKit surfaces against the effective appearance; the selected tab has its own subtle semantic tint. The macOS test suite and `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` pass. A URL-added server appeared Healthy, opened the RepoOS sign-in page, and remained saved after relaunch. Nick’s login is required for authenticated UI verification.

## Work and rationale

The app launched without crashing. In Dark appearance, the sidebar was white while its row labels and URLs were light, making all but the selected row unreadable. Count badges had weak contrast, and the sidebar was too narrow to show full server details. The selected `localhost:7405` entry was Offline with “Start local server.”

The source mixed an explicit white shell for the System preference with SwiftUI’s system color scheme. AppKit window and content layers were also assigned concrete colors, allowing them to drift from SwiftUI’s effective appearance. The fix resolves semantic `NSColor.windowBackgroundColor` against the effective Aqua or Dark Aqua appearance and shares that shell color across the content, sidebar, and tab strip. An appearance notification repaints native layers using each window’s effective appearance, avoiding reliance on global defaults that may lag the notification. Server names use the semantic primary foreground, and the sidebar now has enough width for its name and URL.

Review round 1 caught a separate visual regression: the selected tab and strip had become the same color. The tab now uses a subtle translucent tint from semantic label color, distinct from the strip and suitable for either appearance. Tests exercise the shell resolver and selected-tab surface in both Aqua and Dark Aqua.

History points to `bf428a0f0` (“fix(macos): render light native chrome explicitly”, 2026-09-26) as the origin of the explicit light chrome behavior; it predates the reported late-October onset. Recent macOS history did not reveal an API change explaining the visual failure. The app probes `/api/health` at the entered origin. There was no listener on port 7405, while the local server on 7171 responded Healthy. The 7405 Offline state was accurate, not a stale status or wrong endpoint.

## Approaches tried

I built and launched the current scheme to reproduce the actual symptom, inspected the native appearance and SwiftUI surfaces, and centralized semantic color resolution. A separately identified test build was used for GUI interaction so the installed Hub was not quit. In dark System appearance, the sidebar and row text became readable, badges regained contrast, and the right edge was no longer clipped. Forced Light appearance showed a light sidebar with dark text. The preference was restored to System.

I added `127.0.0.1:7171` through the Add Server flow. The app showed it as Healthy and opened the RepoOS login page. After quitting and relaunching the test app, the server remained saved and Healthy. This alias remains in the user’s Hub registry. Authentication was not attempted; Nick’s credentials are needed to inspect the UI behind sign-in.

The first macOS test run exposed discovery tests that inherited the real `~/.repoos/servers` registry, preventing their fallback-scan fixtures from running. I isolated these tests with a unique nonexistent registry directory and made the populated-registry test assert that fallback scanning does not occur.

## Challenges and blockers

The full macOS `xcodebuild ... test` suite passed after the change, including the new two-appearance surface regression test. The focused selected-tab test also passed. `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed the changed-path validation, including format, lint, build, UI smoke, and remote tests.

Xcode printed a CoreDevice private-framework symbol warning and a CoreSimulator version warning, but both macOS builds and test runs succeeded. No crash occurred, so there is no crash log. Port 7405 was unavailable; 7171 provided a live URL test. The app reached the login screen, and further verification needs Nick to authenticate.

## Key learnings

System appearance must be resolved where AppKit colors become concrete layer colors; a hard-coded light surface under a System preference can conflict with SwiftUI’s dark text and controls. Related surfaces should share the same appearance resolution while retaining distinct roles such as the selected-tab pill. Tests should control registry paths instead of depending on developer machine state. Checking the actual listener and a known-good server URL distinguishes a legitimate Offline state from a health-probe regression.
